      <title>Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/vw-ford-tesla-batteries-deforestation-indigenous-lands</link>
      <description><p>Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia</p><p>Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction.</p><p>Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2026/oct/16/vw-ford-tesla-batteries-deforestation-indigenous-lands">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy</link>
      <description><p>As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/15/what-is-your-personal-recession-indicator">Tell us: what is your personal ‘recession indicator’?</a></p></li></ul><p>When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries. “If I want sushi, I’m getting sushi,” said the 24-year-old nanny, who lives in Raleigh, North Carolina. “I’m definitely lazy in that regard.”</p><p>Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/food/2026/oct/15/food-delivery-apps-cost-economy">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Is punishing the poor Trump’s last hand to play?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms</link>
      <description><p>The pre-midterm defenestration of ACA enrollees looks like political madness – but the president appears to believe hitting poor people might work for him</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/community/live/2026/oct/14/us-economy-affordability-midterm-elections-republicans-trump">Our reporters answer your questions on whether Trump’s economy will sink Republicans in the US midterms</a></p></li></ul><p>There is a manic quality to <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s desperate dash to do something, anything, ahead of November’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/us-midterm-elections-2026">midterm elections</a> to convince beleaguered Americans that he can make the pressures his policies have imposed on their livelihoods go away.</p><p>The US president <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/28/trump-cattle-ranchers-beef-imports-backlash">offered</a> to lower barriers against beef imports to limit surging meat prices, only to consider <a href="https://www.politico.com/news/2026/09/23/trump-beef-imports-midterms-gop-panic-01090261">backtracking</a> under <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/aug/25/trump-republican-backlash-beef-tariff-import">pressure</a> from the cow lobby. He <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/22/trump-diesel-export-ban">offered</a> to stop diesel exports, only to find oil companies <a href="https://finance.yahoo.com/energy/articles/market-chatter-us-oil-executives-112235250.html">were</a> <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/chevron-ceo-diesel-export-ban-trump-supply.html">not interested</a>. He weakened fuel efficiency standards, claiming this would trim the price of a new car (and forgetting to point out it will also raise spending on gas). In early October he started mailing <a href="https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/01/economy/trump-obamacare-500-check">$500 checks</a> to nearly a million people touting his healthcare “wins”. Oh, and he promised adult Americans a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-5000-midterm-cash-dividend-response">$5,000 check</a> if Republicans maintain control of Congress. That, too, will <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/10/trump-dividend-republican-midterm-convention">go nowhere</a>.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/oct/13/trump-aca-healthcare-politics-midterms">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/who-hacked-frances-supermarket-fridges</link>
      <description><p>Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers</p><p>Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise.</p><p>In a <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/12/cyber-attack-defrosts-refrigerators-france-supermarket-chains-intermarche-cooperative-u">“bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack,</a> hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/oct/17/who-hacked-frances-supermarket-fridges">Continue reading...</a></description>
      <category domain="https://www.theguardian.com/world/france">France</category>

<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 20 Oct 2026 14:23:16 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[Ryanair chief Michael O’Leary predicts 20% increase in airfares next year]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/ryanair-chief-michael-oleary-predicts-20-increase-in-air-fares-next-year/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/ryanair-chief-michael-oleary-predicts-20-increase-in-air-fares-next-year/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 09:51:46 +0000Ryanair Holdings chief executive Michael O’Leary predicted a record increase in European air fares next year as the Middle East war continues to drive up oil prices, forcing airlines to pass on their fuel costs to consumers.

Ticket prices are set to increase by as much as 20 per cent next year, O’Leary said on Tuesday during a press conference in Brussels. As a result, airline margins will get squeezed because even the jump in fuel surcharges won’t make up for the higher oil bill, he said.

“You’re going to see the biggest increase in airfares, I would say, in history in Europe in the next 12 months,” O’Leary said. “The question is, will that increase in airfares be enough to cover the dramatically higher oil bills? I don’t think it will be.”

The comments by the head of Europe’s largest budget carrier add to the more pessimistic outlook for the aviation industry, which has been forced to contend with a dramatic jump in costs even as travellers continue to splurge on air tickets.

O’Leary said most European airlines, including his own, lack significant hedging next year to protect against higher oil prices. In addition, there’s less capacity in the market as some airlines struggle, while higher taxes are further dimming the picture for the industry.

Ryanair doesn’t expect big delivery delays on Boeing software issue

“We’re 85 per cent unhedged next year, and most of the other European airlines are in a similar position,” he said.

Ryanair dropped as much as 2.2 per cent in morning trading in Dublin, bringing the decline to about 25 per cent for the year. At that rate, that would be the worst annual stock return since 2018.

O’Leary used his expletive-laden press conference to dish out against regulation in markets like France and Belgium, where Ryanair will reduce its footprint in response to higher taxes. He reiterated that the European aviation industry will continue to consolidate as weaker players struggle to survive in a high-cost environment.

Air Baltic Corp and Spain’s Volotea are the latest European carriers to undergo restructuring as higher costs take their toll. Last week, Lufthansa won the race against Air France-KLM to acquire a stake in Portugal’s state-owned TAP. Meanwhile, US private equity firm Apollo Global Management is laying out the framework to take over British carrier EasyJet.

Airlines across the world have suffered from soaring jet fuel costs since the Iran war began in late February. Ryanair’s most recent earnings in July showed the conflict hit its profit and caused later bookings amid concern about jet-fuel supply availability.

O’Leary said separately that he aims to receive the first delivery of the carrier’s Boeing Max 10 aircraft in January, with about 16 more expected through April. – Bloomberg

]]>Olivier Hoslet<![CDATA[Paddy Power owner Flutter to cut 240 Irish jobs at Irish head office]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/paddy-power-owner-flutter-to-axe-1400-jobs-in-dublin-and-leeds/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/paddy-power-owner-flutter-to-axe-1400-jobs-in-dublin-and-leeds/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 12:18:58 +0000Paddy Power owner Flutter will cut 240 jobs from its Irish head office as it grapples with rising British betting taxes.

The group said on Tuesday that it planned to cut around 1,400 jobs in its UK and Ireland division to counter the impact of British government tax rises set to cost it $540 million (€481 million).

Around 240 of those jobs will be lost in its Dublin office, while the group will also cut workforce numbers in the UK and in various centres around Europe, according to sources familiar with the group.

Flutter did not comment on the numbers that will be lost in each location.

However an industry source estimated that more than 500 jobs could go in the UK, with the remaining cuts in Porto, Portugal, and Cluj-Napoca, Romania, Malta and Gibraltar, which service the UK and Ireland division.

Gaming and betting duty hikes announced by Britain’s Labour government will cost Flutter’s UK and Ireland unit $540 million this year, the group has already confirmed.

Its business in the Republic, which includes bookmaker Paddy Power, is hit as it forms part of the UK and Ireland division.

UK and Ireland chief executive Kevin Harrington said the group was not able to “fully absorb” the impact without cutting costs.

Paddy Power’s long goodbye from betting shops accelerates

Plans announced in last year’s UK autumn budget saw the rate of remote gaming duty – the tax on online casino games and slots – increase from 21 per cent to 40 per cent earlier this year.

Firms will also see a new 25 per cent rate of general betting duty for online bets from April next year, up from 15 per cent, as part of the budget changes.

It comes amid speculation that UK prime minister Andy Burnham’s government could increase the rate of machine games duty, which is the tax on fruit machines, roulette machines and other slot machines, at the next budget later this month.

Flutter said its restructuring plan is likely to cost between $80 million (€71 million) and $90 million.

Harrington said: “The material increase in betting and gaming duties announced in the UK budget last year has fundamentally changed the economic model of the regulated betting and gaming industry in the UK while helping to fuel the unlicensed, unregulated market.

“As we warned a year ago, we cannot fully absorb a rise of this magnitude without reducing our fixed cost base and therefore must restructure our business so that we can best position ourselves for the future.

“We remain confident that we are well placed to benefit from share gains given our position as the largest scale operator in the UK.” – Additional reporting: PA

]]>Bloomberg<![CDATA[Millions affected by Revolut disruption linked to Google Cloud outage]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/revolut-services-hit-by-outage-including-in-ireland/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/10/20/revolut-services-hit-by-outage-including-in-ireland/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 08:52:55 +0000Millions of customers of digital bank Revolut have reported problems accessing the bank’s systems, with the disruption hitting multiple services.

The disruption was linked to an outage at Google Cloud, which provides core infrastructure services to Revolut.

The problems began earlier this morning, with DownDetector recording a spike in reports between 7 and 8am. Customers reported issues accessing the app and transferring funds, but other reports indicated card payments and cash withdrawals were also affected.

]]>matejmo<![CDATA[More market disruption ahead as streamers go after live sports]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/10/20/more-market-disruption-ahead-as-streamers-go-after-live-sports/https://www.irishtimes.com/media/2026/10/20/more-market-disruption-ahead-as-streamers-go-after-live-sports/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 05:00:01 +0000People have been predicting for a while now that it was only a matter of time before the big streaming platforms got serious about disrupting the lucrative live sports market. Until fairly recently, they seemed more interested in one-off marquee events than in longer-term licences. That’s now changing.

Netflix executives spent years explaining why they didn’t need sport. Their first live forays were deliberately eye-catching: a Mike Tyson comeback fight here, a couple of NFL games on Christmas Day there. Then came a 10-year $5 billion deal for WWE wrestling, a slice of Major League Baseball and now the biggest football tournament on the planet in one of its main markets (Spain holds both the men’s and women’s World Cup titles).

Why the change of heart? Partly because Netflix and its rivals have run out of easy growth in mature markets. Keeping existing subscribers is just as important as finding new ones, and sport is the most reliable antidote for churn. People who binge a drama often cancel when it ends, but people who follow a team tend to stay for the whole season.

Then there’s advertising. Every big streamer now offers a cheaper tier carrying ads, and advertisers will pay a premium for audiences watching live in large numbers simultaneously. Sport is almost the only programming that delivers that any more. The irony is that the streamers did more than anyone to break the habit of collective, scheduled viewing. Now they are spending heavily to buy it back.

Watching the Premier League in Ireland is a strikingly costly business

The economics of sports rights explains why the price keeps rising inexorably. A league or federation sells something that cannot be replicated by a new entrant (no matter how hard the Saudis try). Rights are carved up by territory, by package and by platform to maximise the number of bidders. Those bidders need the property so badly that they overpay for it. The pay-TV model that Sky built around the Premier League in the 1990s established the principle of sport as the anchor holding an expensive bundle together.

Now the bundle is fraying. According to Ampere Analysis, streaming services will spend about $14.2 billion on sports rights this year. Amazon has overtaken DAZN as the biggest spender, and general entertainment platforms like Amazon, Netflix, Disney+, Apple and Paramount+ now account for 44 per cent of the total, up from 31 per cent last year. Their advantage over a specialist like DAZN, which has lost billions acquiring and distributing rights across Europe and Japan, is that sport doesn’t have to pay for itself. It only has to make the wider subscription more sticky. And a global platform can spread the cost across hundreds of millions of customers.

Netflix will make one match each day free to watch, and will sub-licence a package to a free-to-air channel that includes every Spain game, both semi-finals and the final. Nor does the law permit it. Under the EU’s audiovisual media rules, member states can draw up lists of events considered so important to society that they must be available on free television. Spain’s 2022 audiovisual law includes the World Cup semi-finals and final. So the Netflix deal recognises that obligation.

Under section 162 of the Broadcasting Act 2009, designated events include the All-Ireland football and hurling finals, Ireland’s games at the World Cup and European Championship along with the opening games, semi-finals and finals of both tournaments. To qualify, a broadcaster must offer a free service reaching more than 90 per cent of the population. These lists were designed to stop Rupert Murdoch putting national shared moments behind a paywall. Whether they are fit for an era when the bidder is a global streamer, possibly one with a free tier of its own, is a question that can’t be avoided forever.

Irish soccer fans are already feeling the effects of fragmentation. From next year, anyone who wants to follow every Champions League game will need RTÉ, Premier Sports, Sky, Amazon Prime Video and Paramount+, which has taken the bulk of the British rights from TNT Sports. RTÉ has held on to its Wednesday night first pick, but it is now one tenant among many. In Gaelic games, GAAGO has shown how quickly matches viewers once took for granted can migrate behind a paywall and how vociferously the public objects when they do. All of this, of course, is welcome news for dodgy box vendors.

The 4.5 per cent growth figure was an improvement on the previous three-month period but it was China’s lowest for decades apart from during the Covid pandemic. Property investment fell by 20.6 per cent in the first nine months of this year and although there are signs of stabilisation in the market in the biggest cities, prices are still falling elsewhere. ]]>Wu Hao<![CDATA[Social-housing pilot guarantees rent for landlords – but will they sign up?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/guaranteed-rent-on-offer-for-landlords-but-will-they-sign-up/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/20/guaranteed-rent-on-offer-for-landlords-but-will-they-sign-up/Tue, 20 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000A new pilot scheme, aimed at boosting the supply of social housing by offering a “secure, low-risk letting option” for landlords, has been launched by the Department of Housing.

Run by councils across Dublin for now, if it’s a success, it might be rolled out across the State.

Announcing the Dublin Rental Accommodation Scheme pilot scheme earlier this year, Minister for Housing, Local Government and Heritage James Browne said: “By encouraging more landlords to make their properties available, the pilot will help increase the supply of homes for individuals and families in need of social housing”.

But how does it work? Is it attractive for landlords? And with the rental market so tight, is it going to be enough to get landlords to commit to social housing?

Run on a pilot basis across the four Dublin local authority areas, the new rental accommodation scheme is being pitched as a “flexible, secure and financially attractive way to let residential properties”.

The tenant target is households that have received rent supplement for 18 months or more, and that have an ongoing housing need. The tenant pays an income-based differential rent contribution to the local authority, and the local authority pays the landlord the agreed rent.

The hope is that if more private landlords sign up for the scheme, more properties should become available to social housing tenants.

What’s different?

This is not the first time councils have looked to incentivise landlords to let their properties through local authorities. The rental accommodation scheme has two components – one working through approved housing boards letting their properties to councils and the other a private-sector arrangement whereby private landlords enter into rental agreements with local authorities.

It is the latter that the new pilot scheme is focusing on.

There have been challenges in attracting and retaining enough properties through the previous scheme. According to a review from the Department of Housing back in 2025, there has been a significant decline in the number of private landlords participating in it.

In 2023, for example, 1,004 landlords left the scheme but just 103 entered, leaving 7,010 tenancies. This compares to 11,231 back in 2018.

Three reasons for this are cited in the report: landlords selling the unit; tenants allocated social housing; and the landlord didn’t renew the contract.

And there are fewer landlords signing up, for reasons including rents on offer that are below market levels.

A spokeswoman for the Irish Property Owners Association (IPOA) says the scheme was “disadvantaged from the start” due to the rules set out in rent pressure zones. The maximum landlords could set rents at through the rental accommodation scheme was 92 per cent of market rent but this made it difficult to get back to a market rate, as only specified increases were allowed.

“It ended up that landlords were actually stuck with that sub-market rate due to rent pressure zones, which made the rent accommodation scheme unappealing,” she says.

HAP (housing assistance payment), on the other hand, had no such limits on the level rent was set at, as councils contribute a fixed amount and the tenant tops up the gap. This made it more attractive to landlords.

As a result, the new rent accommodation scheme pilot has been launched with some key differences. Firstly, landlords can charge local authorities up to 100 per cent of market rent. This rent is guaranteed, and will be paid “in full and on time” by the local authority – not the tenant.

And, if a tenant decides to leave, the council will pay the rent until a new tenant is placed.

Moreover, tenants will be sourced by the local authority, which means landlords won’t have to take on the task of vetting possible tenants.

The maximum length of a contract has also been extended, from four-to-six years previously to eight under the pilot scheme.

Rental payments will be front-loaded, so landlords won’t have to wait for their first payment. There will be better damage and compensation arrangements. And applications for the scheme will be more streamlined. Landlords will be responsible for managing the tenancy, and the property.

Is it enough?

County councils certainly hope it is. Pamela Kearns, mayor of South Dublin County Council, says the scheme will transform lives.

“Every property made available provides a vulnerable family, individual or senior with a safe, stable home in our community. While Dublin desperately needs housing, it also thrives on collaboration. Landlords now have a meaningful way to tackle housing shortages and build stronger communities. It is a true win for owners, tenants and Dublin as a whole.”

Already there has been “significant” interest in the new pilot, says the Department of Housing, with about 200 applications received by the end of September.

However, while the new scheme may have some key differences, groups representing property owners say it may not be enough to encourage landlords out of the private market and into guaranteed rent through the rental accommodation scheme.

“It looks very well on paper, but once you scratch the surface it’s not really like that,” says the spokeswoman for the IPOA, adding that there are a “couple of hurdles” that are making it unpalatable for landlords.

Firstly, the promise of full market rent is a “marketing strategy”, says the spokeswoman, because under the current legislation, a landlord can only charge market rent if they’re eligible for it, such as at the end of a six-year tenancy cycle. And if you’re not eligible then the council cannot override Residential Tenancies Board (RTB) rules.

Another issue is the length of the contract. A contract of a maximum eight years could mean that smaller landlords (ie those with four or fewer properties) could end up with a tenant for 12 years – even if the council drops out after eight. And larger landlords could have the tenant for life even if the council is no longer involved.

And if the tenancy wasn’t working out, such as if the tenant stopped paying rent, the IPOA spokeswoman says the landlord would need to go down the standard legal route, and issue a notice of termination. But it can take up to two years to get vacant possession of the property, she says.

However, the spokesman for the Department of Housing says tenancies can match up and “a six-year rent accommodation scheme agreement can align with the statutory cycle for small landlords with one to three tenancies, provided the relevant start dates coincide”.

For larger tenants, however, these new tenancies can only be ended for breaches of tenant obligations or because the property no longer meets the needs of the household’s accommodation needs.

Another challenge that might arise is that although the landlord doesn’t select their tenant, if things go wrong, they still have to sort it out. “The main landlord-tenant relationship ultimately remains the same between the property owner and the rental accommodation scheme tenant as it would with a typical private rented tenancy,” the scheme’s documentation states.

Forward payment is just two months, while other benefits can’t really be described as such, the IPOA argues. The offer of “100 per cent mortgage interest tax relief” is something all landlords are entitled to – while property tax is not eligible for a tax deduction.

Another factor, says the spokeswoman, is that the rental accommodation scheme has “very, very strict property standards enforcement”.

If an issue is identified – and according to the spokeswoman it could be something as relatively minor as the width set on window restrictors – rent payments will be suspended until the landlord gets its sorted.

The scheme is being run on a pilot basis until 2029 to see whether or not this additional flexibility will result in an increased flow of properties.

“This pilot allows us to test whether additional flexibility and stronger supports can increase property owner participation and expand the supply of homes available to social housing tenants,” the Minister said, adding that the results of the scheme would guide future national policy.

]]>Marc O'Sullivan<![CDATA[Why London looks better than ever for a business shindig]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/19/why-london-looks-better-than-ever-for-a-business-shindig/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/10/19/why-london-looks-better-than-ever-for-a-business-shindig/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 05:00:00 +0000As deadly Houthi missiles smashed into Riyadh’s international airport last week, people from around the world still made their way to the Saudi capital for one of the biggest oil and gas industry conferences on the calendar.

The bosses of ExxonMobil, TotalEnergies, Shell and BP had pulled out after the attacks, which killed at least a dozen people and injured hundreds more.

I expect more big names will skip another international conference due to start in a week in Riyadh – the so-called Davos in the Desert.

This probably won’t be the last time this happens in a complicated world showing no sign of improvement. A string of Middle East trade shows and conventions has already been cancelled or deferred as the Iran war grinds on. The street arrests and travel restrictions by Donald Trump’s administration continue to drive international academic conferences away from the US to other countries.

As a frequent conference-goer myself, these dispiriting sights have made me wonder: which cities are now deemed the best places for business gatherings?

To my surprise, it turns out I am living in one of them.

London was named the best city in Europe for events and meetings this year for the fourth year in a row in a closely watched ranking by the Cvent conference tech group.

Yet again we beat Barcelona, Madrid and Lisbon. Even Paris only managed fifth place.

I say “we”, even though I am a transplanted Australian, one of the more than 40 per cent of Londoners who are foreign-born. As it happens, that is a higher share than you will find in Paris, Berlin and even New York City – a pleasing reminder that London is one of the most diverse major cities on the planet.

Cvent makes scant mention of this in its list of reasons for ranking London so highly. But the factors it does cite underscore how revealing it is to look at your city as an outsider.

The sprawling conference centres I am occasionally required to trek out to for work are apparently world-class.

London Southend Airport, which I have never technically been to, means we have six airports. There are also more than 80 Michelin-starred restaurants and, by Cvent’s count, 200 museums, 270 theatres, 857 art galleries and four Unesco World Heritage sites. If you are wondering, they are the Tower of London, the Palace (and Abbey) of Westminster, Kew Gardens, and maritime Greenwich.

All this helps to explain why the London Convention Bureau, a division of the city’s official growth agency, is expecting close to 80,000 convention visitors this year. Thousands of rheumatologists and urologists have already been for their latest shindigs. The 44th World Scout Conference is due next year, along with hundreds of port and harbour delegates and a slew of tech conventions.

The striking thing is, the big draws for convention delegates are just a fraction of what London now offers its full-time residents.

As of this year, there is year-round outdoor swimming in, of all places, Canary Wharf. You can get there on the Elizabeth Line railway that has transformed cross-city travel. Or cycle there via the cycle superhighways that have revolutionised two-wheeled transport.

Or take the Tube that we all moan about constantly, and is admittedly expensive, but still zips you across the city in a sliver of the time it takes to cover such distances in other big cities. And you don’t even need to queue up for a ticket. Just swipe a credit card on the turnstile.

Next week, something even more astonishing will begin. After years of wrangling and false starts, a stretch of Oxford Street nearly 1km long will be closed to traffic as the famed shopping street at long last starts to become pedestrianised.

Is London ‘lawless’ or the safest big city in the western world? Take your pick

As usual, critics are predicting mayhem. Diverted traffic will clog side streets. Bin collections won’t work. People will feel unsafe at night, and so on.

I suspect the doubters will all be proved wrong and the move will be so successful that we will regret it not happening years ago.

At least I hope so. Watching a city brighten and improve is a pleasure for visitors and residents alike. At a time when war and political strife stalk ever more unlikely places, these are gains that should be celebrated – and never taken for granted. – Copyright The Financial Times

To judge by the rows over recent decades about the EU’s budget, you might believe it is a major drain on member states’ national resources. However, the budget amounts to only 1.1 per cent of national income, whereas national budgets across the EU average 45 per cent of national income, somewhat higher than for Ireland.

So the fight over whether the budget should amount to 1 per cent or 1.25 per cent of national income is about relatively small sums when averaged across the EU. In national budgets, such a small difference as a share of national income could get lost in rounding errors.

There are a range of public goods that are best undertaken on a pan-EU basis rather than by national governments. Examples include cross-border infrastructure, research and development, climate, security, foreign policy, industrial policy and development aid. These are areas where collective EU spending is more effective than uncoordinated national investment.

European Commission unhappy with EU budget but Taoiseach says compromise had to be made

The construction of the electricity interconnector between Ireland and France is a prime example that merits the significant EU funding involved. This project will benefit not only Ireland and France, but also the wider EU electricity system.

Interconnection across borders boosts efficiency, provides better matching of variable supply and demand, and minimises wasted power generation.

Other potentially beneficial projects to enable the free flow of electricity across the EU’s national boundaries are only likely to proceed if there is EU financial support.

Food shortages in the aftermath of the second World War were the initial driving force behind the EU’s Common Agricultural Policy. Today, however, it is more difficult to justify rationally why agriculture looms so large in the EU’s budget, or why the EU rather than national governments should fund farm supports.

Europe rearms: files reveal extent of plans for a new ‘defence union’

Ireland, of course, has benefited disproportionately from EU payments to farmers over the past half century. Like other EU members, we pay about 1 per cent of national income into the EU budget. However, despite the fact that we are one of the richest EU members, we get back around 0.7 per cent of national income, most of it going to Irish farmers. A great deal.

The modernising of Ireland’s infrastructure has also benefited greatly from EU support to poorer regions over the first decades of EU membership.

Today there are two groups of countries with very different outlooks on the EU’s budget.

The “frugals”, like Scandinavia, Germany and the Netherlands, want a smaller budget, in particular they want to cut back on funds for agriculture, and for infrastructure in poorer states. They want to reallocate funds to other headings.

The “friends of cohesion”, which include Spain, Italy and some poorer member states, want a larger budget, with continuing substantial agriculture and cohesion payments.

The first stab at a compromise by the Irish presidency involved a small cut in the original EU Commission budget proposal. For 2028-34, this proposed that real EU resources, after debt interest, would be slightly lower than today.

The Irish Times view on the EU budget: a key task for Ireland’s presidency

This draft also largely protected agriculture and cohesion funds. But this compromise got a widespread thumbs down.

In the next round of negotiations, Ireland needs to adjust its proposals to garner more support. Next time, the Bruegel think tank in Brussels suggests, we should propose a slightly larger budget that cuts back on agriculture and cohesion funds, which are unpopular with the frugals, and that reallocates some resources to other European public goods.

A few rounds of proposals may be needed to garner the necessary majority support before year end.

As the honest broker, it may thus fall to the Irish Government to propose a compromise budget that would cut some resources for agriculture, which will be unpopular at home.

However, given the risk that delayed agreement could mean an even more unpalatable outcome, as the political winds shift in France and elsewhere, it is vital from an Irish point of view that agreement is reached on the budget by the end of the year. Better a budget with somewhat reduced funds for agriculture, than no budget and no funds.

]]>LockieCurrie<![CDATA[AI fever is producing some strange symptoms]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/19/ai-fever-is-producing-some-strange-symptoms/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/10/19/ai-fever-is-producing-some-strange-symptoms/Mon, 19 Oct 2026 04:00:00 +0000“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” Broadcom chief executive Hock Tan warned this week, saying they set “very extreme expectations” only to discover that the AI trade resembles a casino.

The comments were unusually forthright, although a few critical remarks would not normally be enough to send shares in mega-cap technology giants such as Samsung (down 7.4 per cent on the day) and SK Hynix (down 10.1 per cent) tumbling.

In truth, there was more to the declines than Tan’s comments, with concerns about Chinese competition, the sustainability of AI spending and Samsung’s latest earnings report all weighing on the sector, but the swings certainly highlighted the fragility of AI-related sentiment.

Meanwhile, Tan’s reference to “very extreme expectations” may have been aimed at investors, but extraordinary expectations of AI are apparently evident elsewhere in the industry. Shyam Sankar, chief technology officer of data analytics giant Palantir, claims some AI researchers have taken up smoking to signal their conviction that artificial intelligence would eventually cure cancer – an example, he said, of the “mass psychosis” and “social delusion” around AI.

Then there is Anthropic, which is moving to prohibit sustained cruelty towards its Claude chatbot, despite the absence of evidence that the software experiences suffering.

Clueless investors with extreme expectations are one thing, but researchers smoking in anticipation of a cure for cancer and developers worrying about a chatbot’s feelings suggest the AI boom is acquiring some distinctly unusual characteristics.

A member of Poland’s military reserve force has been detained for alleged espionage.

On Monday afternoon, following media reports of the arrest, a spokesman for the military police confirmed that they had detained a 31-year-old man of Polish and Ukrainian citizenship, who holds the rank of senior private reserve.

The suspect, who had at the time been undertaking a course at the Military Medical Academy (WAM) in Łódź, is being held on suspicion of declaring readiness to act for the benefit of a foreign intelligence service against Poland. That crime is punishable by up to eight years in prison.

W dniu 16 października 2026 r. żołnierze z Oddziału Żandarmerii Wojskowej w Łodzi, zgodnie z postanowieniem Prokuratora Działu do Spraw Wojskowych Prokuratury Rejonowej Łódź-Polesie w Łodzi, dokonali zatrzymania mężczyzny w wieku 31 lat, obywatelstwa polskiego i ukraińskiego, w… pic.twitter.com/MLpqzfT4iO

— Żandarmeria Wojskowa (@Zandarmeria) October 19, 2026

The Polish authorities have not revealed which foreign intelligence service the suspect – who has been placed in detention for three months – is believed to be associated with.

Speaking later to reporters, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk said that the man had “clearly shown himself to be someone who is conducting reconnaissance of certain types of military installations belonging to the Polish armed forces”. He also revealed that the suspect had recently obtained Polish citizenship.

While the authorities have not released further information, Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, reported earlier on Monday that the suspect, whom it named as Vasiliy, had been found in possession of several different phones, documents, and a large amount of money and gold.

 

Poland has recently seen a number of high-profile cases of individuals charged – and in some cases convicted – of spying on behalf of Russia and Belarus.

Poland’s security services recently revealed that the number of espionage cases they launched last year was more than double the figure for 2024. Over those two years combined, there were more investigations than in the previous three decades.

This month, a former Polish soldier was sentenced to five and a half years for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland.

A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia.

He was tasked with reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa while he travelled through Poland https://t.co/WCmhyHG1Kp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

In July, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb.

In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force (WOT) with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops.

In December last year, a Russian national was charged with running an espionage and sabotage network in Poland on behalf of Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB). The agents whom he oversaw were mainly Ukrainians and Belarusians, as have been many others convicted of conducting Russian hybrid activities in Poland.

]]> Poland expels 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in Karate World Championships https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/19/poland-expels-15-russians-and-belarusians-who-tried-to-take-part-in-karate-world-championships/ Mon, 19 Oct 2026 21:11:35 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105721

Poland has detained and expelled 15 Russians and Belarusians who tried to take part in youth world karate championships that were taking place in the Polish city of Bielsko-Biała.

“Eleven Belarusian citizens and four Russians entered the country on tourist visas, which was inconsistent with the declared purpose of their stay in Poland,” said border guard spokesman Szymon Mościcki.

After being detained, they received orders to leave the country within eight days, which is “the shortest possible deadline”, he added, quoted by broadcaster TVP.

Piętnastu obywateli Rosji i Białorusi zostało zatrzymanych przez Straż Graniczną. Przyjechali do Polski na wizach turystycznych, choć prawdopodobnie zamierzali wziąć udział w mistrzostwach świata w karate. Otrzymali decyzje nakazujące opuszczenie kraju.https://t.co/czcjQKZ2kw

— tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) October 19, 2026

The announcement came one day after the karate world championships in the cadet, junior and U-21 categories had finished in Bielsko-Biała.

In early October, Russia’s TASS news agency had reported that some of the country’s junior karatekas, as competitors are known, had planned to compete in the tournament. The World Karate Federation (WKF) allows Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under a neutral banner.

However, Poland has a strict policy of not allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete in tournaments on its territory. This year, it banned them from taking part in a World Cup ski jumping event. It was also removed as host of two European junior weightlifting championships for banning Russian and Belarusian athletes.

 

On 15 October, the day after the championships in Bielsko-Biała had started, TASS reported that none of the Russian athletes had been allowed to register by the Polish organisers.

Paweł Połtorzecki, president of the Polish Karate Union (PUK), confirmed that, despite PUK warning them not to come, Russian and Belarusian athletes had sought to take part, prompting the organisers to ask the border guard to conduct an inspection.

“The first sign was the appearance of a Russian at the refereeing course,” he revealed, quoted by TVP. “That’s when the first detention occurred.”

Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading Polish daily, reports that the Russian karatekas had obtained tourist visas from other countries in the European Schengen area, of which Poland is part. Poland itself does not issue tourist visas to Russians.

Poland has been removed as the host of two European junior weightlifting championships after refusing to allow Russian athletes to take part

The European Weightlifting Federation says it "does not accept discrimination based on geopolitical circumstances" https://t.co/j7PfiTHZ1M

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 9, 2026

Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has been one of Kyiv’s closest allies, providing military and humanitarian support while also pressing for tougher international sanctions against Moscow.

Meanwhile, Poland has become the primary target in Europe for sabotage operations carried out by operatives working on behalf of Russia, including arson attacks and an attempt to derail a train. Russia has also repeatedly violated Polish airspace with drones, missiles and, most recently, a helicopter.

In response to Russia’s aggressive actions, Poland has successively shut down all Russian consulates on its territory. Moscow responded by likewise closing all Polish consulates that it previously hosted. In January, Russia warned its citizens against travelling to Poland due to “Russophobia”.

]]> Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/19/poland-breaks-up-international-criminal-group-accused-of-laundering-e77-million/ Mon, 19 Oct 2026 12:48:31 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105678

Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams.

Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty.

Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP

— Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026

The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation.

The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted.

Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures.

Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies.

 

“The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.”

The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation.

Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland.

]]> Lithuania says Ukrainian drone that struck car entered its airspace from Poland https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/19/lithuania-says-ukrainian-drone-that-struck-car-entered-its-airspace-from-poland/ Mon, 19 Oct 2026 11:53:47 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105676

This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon.

Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia.

Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU.

This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace.

What appears to be a drone exploded…

— Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026

On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object.

President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”.

Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace.

“I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT.

 

However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”.

Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country.

In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”.

Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”.

We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia.

We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have…

— Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026

Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian.

“We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.”

The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was.

Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming.

On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself.

It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place.

Poland’s energy ministry has signed an agreement with two state-owned companies, Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) and Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE), setting out responsibilities for preparing for the construction of Poland’s planned second nuclear power plant.

“This is an investment in our security, sovereignty and economic development,” declared energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Having our own stable energy sources strengthens Poland’s resilience to crises and reduces dependence on external suppliers.”

Polska jest 20. gospodarką świata, ale nasze ambicje sięgają wyżej. Nie będzie silnej, niezależnej gospodarki bez… pic.twitter.com/eQ7zWFEolh

— Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) October 13, 2026

Under the agreement, PEJ, which is also responsible for developing a first nuclear project that is already underway on Poland’s northern Baltic Sea coast, will act as the investor and coordinate the project.

PGE, the country’s largest power producer, will prepare preliminary feasibility studies and analyse potential locations for the plant.

However, a decision on selecting an international partner for the project is not expected to be made until next year. The potential candidates include US company Westinghouse, which is involved in the first nuclear power plant, France’s EDF, and Canada’s AtkinsRéalis.

 

The second plant was initially envisaged as a joint project with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a South Korean company, under a letter of intent signed in 2022 under Poland’s former government. However, the partnership was never formalised and fell through last year.

Once the new partner has been selected, it will work with PGE to analyse potential sites. The current preferred locations are Bełchatów – home to the largest coal-fired power station in Europe, owned by PGE – and Konin, both in central Poland, because of their existing energy infrastructure and experience in electricity generation.

According to the Polish government’s nuclear strategy – which was last month updated for the first time since 2020 – construction of the second plant is scheduled to begin in 2032, with its first reactor potentially entering service in 2040. That would be one year behind the previously planned schedule.

The government has updated Poland's nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new plan confirming that the first nuclear plant will launch three years later than previously planned, in 2036, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule https://t.co/vgtuSXLDjZ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 3, 2026

Meanwhile, Poland plans to begin construction of its first nuclear power station in 2028, with the plant beginning operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Together, the two plants are expected to have a combined capacity of up to 9 gigawatts.

The move is part of Poland’s transition away from coal – which still generates around half of electricity, by far the highest proportion in the European Union – and towards cleaner sources of energy, particularly nuclear and renewables.

Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%).

]]> Everything you need to know one year ahead of Poland’s parliamentary elections https://notesfrompoland.com/2026/10/15/everything-you-need-to-know-one-year-ahead-of-polands-parliamentary-elections/ Thu, 15 Oct 2026 09:48:11 +0000 https://notesfrompoland.com/?p=105449 Daniel Tilles Polling suggests the outcome is too close to call.]]>

Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!

By Daniel Tilles

Poland will hold parliamentary elections a year from now. The outcome will decide who governs the country for the next four years – although, given how close the polls are, and with questions over coalition formation, it could also result in uncertainty, chaos, and even new elections being called.

Below, we explain how the elections work, which parties will be standing, what kind of outcomes are possible, and which issues may animate the campaign.

When will the election take place?

Assuming early elections are not called, the vote must take place on a non-working day in the last 30 days before the end of the current four-year parliamentary term, which began on 13 November 2023.

Because elections in Poland are held on Sundays, that gives four possible dates: 17, 24 or 31 October, or 7 November (though 1 November and 11 November, which are public holidays, are also theoretically possible).

It is the president, Karol Nawrocki, who will choose the date. He must do so no later than 90 days before the end of the current parliamentary term.

How does voting work?

The 460 members of the more powerful lower house, the Sejm, are elected through proportional representation, meaning that seats are distributed more or less on the basis of the share of the vote parties receive (using the so-called D’Hondt method for allocating seats from electoral lists put forward by each party). However, parties must receive at least 5% of the vote nationally to enter parliament (a figure that rises to 8% for coalitions of parties who stand on a single electoral list).

The 100 members of the upper-house Senate are chosen through a first-past-the-post system similar to how members of the US Congress or British House of Commons are elected, with the candidate in each district that receives the most votes winning the seat.

How is a government formed?

A government can only be formed if it can win a vote of confidence in the Sejm.

After the elections, the president designates a prime minister, who is tasked with forming a government – which would almost certainly be made up of a coalition of parties – that must then win a vote of confidence.

If they fail to do so (as happened in 2023), the Sejm votes to choose an alternative prime minister, who likewise must try to form a government that has the confidence of the Sejm.

Parliament has chosen @donaldtusk as Poland's new prime minister.

That paves the way for him to form a new government in the coming days, ending the eight-year rule of the national-conservative PiS party https://t.co/iZUKh2rxnP

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2023

If that fails, the president has a second chance to pick a prime minister, who must again win a confidence vote. However, whereas the previous two votes require an absolute majority (większość bezwzględna) to be carried, this time only a simple majority is needed, making it easier to form a minority government.

If this third and final attempt does not work, then parliament is dissolved and new elections are called.

Who is likely to form the next government?

At the moment, it is incredibly difficult to say. Polls suggest an even split in support between parties generally aligned with Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition – which ranges from left to centre right – and the right-wing opposition. However, the 5% electoral threshold complicates the picture.

According to current polling averages compiled by Polish website eWybory and Politico Europe, Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) leads with 32%. One of its coalition partners, The Left (Lewica), is on 7%, while two others, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL) and centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), are on around 3% and 1%, respectively. Another left-wing party, Together (Razem), which previously caucused with the ruling coalition but split in 2024, is on around 4%.

Meanwhile, the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), the largest opposition party, is on 20%. Two far-right opposition groups, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), have 14% and 9%, respectively. The right-wing Development Plus (Rozwój Plus), which broke away from PiS this year, is at around 5%.

Rolling 30-day average support in polls for Poland’s main political parties (source: eWybory.eu)

If we treat those as two potential blocs, parties more or less aligned with the current government are on around 47% while the right-wing opposition is on 48%. However, PSL and Poland 2050 currently look likely to fall below the 5% threshold if they stand alone, meaning votes for them would not count. That would significantly harm Tusk’s chances of forming a new government. If Rozwój Plus stood alone and fell below the threshold, that would harm the opposition.

It is therefore likely that, as the elections draw nearer, parties that seem likely to fall below 5% will seek to join forces with other groups. In 2023, PSL and Poland 2050 stood together in the so-called Third Way (Trzecia Droga) alliance. But they have made clear they do not intend to do that again. That leaves them with limited options. They could join forces with KO on a single electoral list, but that does not guarantee that their voters will follow them. Indeed, some may baulk at voting for Tusk’s party.

The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026

Meanwhile, there are some wildcards in the pack. KKP, led by radical-right extremist Grzegorz Braun, is shunned by the mainstream right for its antisemitism, anti-Americanism and sympathy towards Russia. PiS’s leader, Jarosław Kaczyński, has declared that he would not allow Braun to join government. Development Plus has taken a similar position. Both parties value relations with the US and the Trump administration, whose ambassador to Poland has reportedly pushed them to rule out working with Braun.

However, if KKP maintains its current level of support, it looks almost impossible for the opposition to form a parliamentary majority without it, meaning there would be a strong temptation to somehow work with Braun. Kaczyński’s determination to remove Tusk from power may outweigh his dislike of Braun and desire to keep the Americans onside.

The Together party – if it manages to pass the 5% threshold – could likewise represent a challenge for Tusk when forming a coalition, given that it has criticised the government for failing to keep promises on healthcare spending, public sector pay, and liberalising the abortion law.

 

There also remains the possibility of some elements from each camp joining the other side – either entire parties or individual MPs defecting – in order to help form a government.

PiS has long sought to tempt PSL to its side (and recent reports suggest that even President Donald Trump tried to persuade PSL’s leader, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, to do so). It is conceivable that Rozwój Plus could work with parts of the current ruling camp, though its hatred of Tusk would make that very difficult.

All of the difficulties outlined above mean there is a significant chance that it will not be possible for anyone to form a government, necessitating fresh elections – something that has never happened before in Poland. If that happens, it would mean uncertainty and a lack of clear leadership at a time when Poland is facing major security challenges and a worsening fiscal situation.

What about the Senate?

The Senate, like the Sejm, is currently controlled by the ruling coalition. Indeed, Tusk has an even larger majority there than in the lower house, making it harder for the opposition to flip. Although the Senate is much weaker than the Sejm – and control of it does not determine who forms the government – it does have some powers that make it a useful asset.

It can slow down the passage of legislation, though not block it. The Senate also must approve the appointment of certain officials, such as the heads of the Supreme Audit Office (NIK) and the Institute of National Remembrance (IPN), as well as the Commissioner for Human Rights (RPO).

In a rare clash between Poland’s two houses of parliament, in both of which the government has a majority, the Senate has rejected a candidate chosen by the Sejm to become the new head of the state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) https://t.co/QUsqfDNh4s

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 7, 2026

The upper house is also required to approve proposals by the president to hold national referendums. This year, the Senate has twice blocked moves by Nawrocki to hold a referendum on EU climate policies.

In a situation where Tusk’s coalition controlled the Sejm, and was therefore still in government, but the right-wing opposition held the Senate, that would give the president a powerful tool to call referendums on policies important to him and the opposition.

To that end, there have been calls for the right-wing and far-right opposition to form a so-called Senate pact, of the type that Tusk and his allies used to win control of the upper house in 2019 and 2023.

What that means in practice is that the parties forming the pact agree to stand only one candidate between them in each of the 100 Senate districts, making it more likely that they will scoop up votes from supporters of all the parties in the pact and win the winner-takes-all contest.

What role will Nawrocki play in all of this?

Presidents are in theory expected to be non-partisan. In practice, however, they will seek to boost parties or coalitions aligned with them, and with whom it will be easier to work.

Since Nawrocki was elected last year, relations and cooperation between the president and government have reached unprecedently low levels. Within just 10 months, Nawrocki had vetoed more bills than any previous president in history over their entire terms. He has made it abundantly clear that he would prefer to work with a government formed from the right-wing opposition.

During his first year, President Nawrocki has transformed his office into a centre of resistance to the government and become a unifying figure for the fragmented right.

But he faces new challenges moving towards the next election, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/uNYrFOppSp

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 7, 2026

However, the extent to which he will be involved in the election campaign is unclear. Some figures on the right hope that Nawrocki will act as a figurehead, using his positive relations with parties across the right-wing opposition to bring them together.

In practical terms, this could involve him acting as the patron of a Senate pact (something the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet recently said the president was willing to do), as well as helping right-wing parties form a coalition government after the elections.

Nawrocki also continues to enjoy strong approval ratings among the conservative electorate, meaning that his presence during the election campaign could act as a boost for the opposition.

What issues are likely to feature in the campaign?

A major issue will be the question of sovereignty. The right-wing opposition accuses Tusk of being Brussels’ and Berlin’s lapdog, handing over ever more power to the EU and prioritising Germany’s interests over Poland’s.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, argues that PiS is too beholden to the Trump administration and warns that the opposition is pushing Poland towards “Polexit” from the EU, which would leave the country isolated and vulnerable, as well as much poorer.

Those battle lines extend to security policy too, with the Tusk government shifting emphasis towards Europe as a defence partner but PiS insisting that only the US can truly guarantee Poland’s security. Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base has already become highly politicised. If progress stalls, the opposition will blame the government. If Washington confirms that the base will go ahead, Nawrocki will seek to take the credit, based on his good relationship with Trump.

On this point, though, it is worth noting the split within the opposition. While PiS and Rozwój Plus are strongly pro-American, Confederation and, to an even greater extent, KKP, are opposed to a greater US presence in Poland.

President @NawrockiKn says that a planned new permanent US military base in Poland is “confirmed” because his American counterpart, Donald Trump, is “famous for keeping his word”.

He also suggested that the new facility will be called “Fort Trump” https://t.co/uGGJSBe5nr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 23, 2026

Where the right-wing opposition has been united, however, is on pushing for a tougher position towards Ukraine and Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

While tensions have calmed significantly since the crisis sparked in May by President Volodymyr Zelensky naming a military unit after a group that massacred Poles in World War Two, it is likely that relations with Ukraine and the large-scale presence of Ukrainians in Poland will remain important issues during the election campaign.

The ruling coalition, meanwhile, will be keen to emphasise its tough overall approach to immigration, which it says was out of control under the former PiS government. It can point to the falling number of new residence permits being issued, the growing number of deportations, and tougher measures on the Belarus border, including a ban on asylum claims.

Poland has forcibly removed 2,100 foreigners from the country this year, around twice as many as in 2024.

The figures come after the government introduced a tougher new migration policy last year, which has included more deportations of foreign criminals https://t.co/zOBxPLipy8

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 31, 2025

The economy, public finances and cost of living are also likely to be major issues.

As long as the current global energy crisis sparked by the conflict around Iran continues, the opposition will seek to place the blame for record fuel prices on the government. They will also cite large deficits and the ballooning public debt as evidence that Tusk is mismanaging the economy.

The ruling coalition will point to continued strong economic growth and blame Nawrocki, who has vetoed revenue-generating tax bills, for the fiscal situation.

In one of his first policy announcements since being elected on Sunday, the new mayor of Kraków, Poland’s second-largest city, has declared that he will withdraw official patronage of its annual LGBT+ equality march.

Łukasz Gibała, who has been supportive of LGBT+ rights in the past and has previously attended the march, argues that the event has become too “partisan”. He stood for election as an independent and has pledged to depoliticise city hall.

His decision does not prevent the march from taking place. But it means that it no longer has the official support of the city.

Łukasz Gibała: Nie obejmę patronatem Marszu Równości. Polityka progresywna nie zawsze się sprawdza https://t.co/vIw8ZsSPQK

— Radio Kraków (@RadioKrakow) October 12, 2026

Kraków’s equality march, which was first held in 2004, draws thousands of participants when it takes place each year in May. The event is used to demand greater LGBT+ rights in Poland, which is ranked as one of the worst countries in Europe for LGBT+ people.

In 2021, the city’s former mayor, Jacek Majchrowski, became an honorary patron of the march. In 2024, his successor, Aleksander Miszalski, became the first mayor to attend the event, declaring that Kraków should be “a home for everyone”.

However, Miszalski was removed from office earlier this year in a recall referendum, necessitating a new election, which was won by Gibała. He beat Monika Piątkowska, who, like Miszaski, is a member of the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party of Prime Minister Donald Tusk.

Kraków's new mayor has announced that he will attend the city’s LGBT parade next week, something his long-serving predecessor never did.

"I want to build a tolerant Kraków, a home for everyone," says @OlekMiszalski, who took office this week https://t.co/ZQ9SzZiHp4

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 9, 2024

The day after his victory, Gibała was asked by local broadcaster Radio Kraków if he would continue city hall’s patronage of the equality march. The new mayor, who takes office next week, declared that he would not, saying he “will avoid sponsoring events that have a partisan character”.

“I have the impression that, over the past three years or so, the community that organises equality marches has simply become partisan,” said Gibała. “These are people who ran for parliament and local government on the lists of specific political parties.”

Gibała did not indicate who he was referring to. However, one of the organisers of the equality march in Kraków is Magdalena Dropek, who has three times stood as a candidate for The Left (Lewica), one of the groups in Tusk’s ruling coalition, in elections to the Polish and European parliaments.

 

Gibała emphasised that he has himself attended equality marches in the past “and does not regret it”. He was previously an MP for both KO (when it was known as Civic Platform, PO) as well as for the liberal Palikot’s Movement (Ruch Palikota), later known as Your Movement (Twój Ruch).

During the recent mayoral election campaign, Gibała told broadcaster TVN that, as an MP, he had supported the introduction of same-sex civil partnerships in Poland, and said that his views had not changed.

When asked if that meant that, as mayor, he would continue the city’s practice of transcribing foreign same-sex marriages into the civil registry – as Poland was ordered to do last year by the Court of Justice of the European Union – Gibała said that he would.

However, he added that he was doing this as a “legalist” who respects the current legal situation. “If a different political party wins [parliamentary elections] next year and changes the law in Poland, it [recognition of foreign same-sex marriages] won’t happen,” he told Radio Kraków.

In fact, although the current government supports recognition of foreign-same sex marraiges, it has not changed the law in that regard. Polish law still does not recognise any form of same-sex union.

The government, aware that opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki would veto any change to the law, instead issued a regulation (which does not require presidential approval) empowering local authorities to transcribe foreign same-sex marriages into their registries.

Many municipalities, especially more liberal larger cities, have begun to do so (some even did before the regulation was issued). But others, especially in more conservative places, have refused to, often arguing that there are legal doubts around the issue.

Data provided to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) by the digital affairs ministry last week showed that 516 foreign same-sex marriages have so far been registered in Poland. The largest numbers were in Warsaw (209), Wrocław (73) and Kraków (46).

The Polish government has granted same-sex couples who married abroad the same tax rights as other married couples

It follows an EU court ruling ordering Poland to recognise such marriages even though domestic law does not allow any form of same-sex union https://t.co/3gE1PQU9AQ

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 25, 2026

In the same interview this week with Radio Kraków, Gibała was asked if he would “return to your political roots” and be a “progressive mayor”. He responded by saying that, while “there are some issues where progressive policies actually work, there are others where they don’t”.

Asked for an example of the latter, Gibała said that, “if we look, for example, at what’s happening in western European cities, there are entire neighbourhoods in which there is a fear of entering for people of our skin colour”.

Prem Rugby will this week announce Thatchers as a new commercial partner as Elton John’s Rocket Sports agency continues to hunt for league sponsors, City AM understands.

The English top flight counts London Pride as its beer sponsor but will add the West Country brand to its partnership roster as official cider partner.

It is part of a push to expand the commercial portfolio of Prem Rugby after onboarding Rocket Sports, which is owned by Crocodile Rock songsmith John. 

Rocket Sports counts the likes of Sir Jason Kenny and Dame Laura Kenny within its athlete management division.

The firm is in the market on behalf of Prem Rugby to seek sponsors for English rugby union’s top competition. Its title partner, insurance giant Gallagher, currently pays an annual high seven-figure sum having extended its deal with Prem Rugby in 2024.

Thatchers pour into Prem Rugby

The Thatchers deal follows recent sponsorship renewals with ball-maker Gilbert and trading platform Etoro. The likes of Defender, Funding Circle and Buffalo Trace feature within the wider portfolio.

Thatchers already has a presence in the Gallagher Prem, sponsoring West Country duo Bath and Bristol Bears as well as East Midlands side Leicester. It also features as a sponsor of both Sussex and Somerset County Cricket Clubs, as well as Hampshire and the Utilita Bowl, which will host one of England cricket’s Ashes Tests next summer.

The cider brand, based at Myrtle Farm in Somerset, earlier this year posted turnover of £124m for the year to August 2025, with profits touching £17m.

But its Companies House filings warned that “the regulatory and taxation environment is becoming increasingly complex and burdensome”, adding that “upcoming taxes and levies continue to add uncertainty to the financial strain”.

They concluded: “Collectively, these factors make operating within the industry more challenging, increasing costs for producers and ultimately impacting affordability for customers.”
