In June 2024, EU-Startups reported on Sirona’s €6 million seed funding round to support the development and deployment of its direct-air-capture systems.

Germany’s Reverion

  • Founded in 2022 as a spinout from the Technical University of Munich, is developing reversible power plants capable of converting gases such as biogas and hydrogen into electricity, while also enabling electricity to be stored through gas production.
  • The company has featured several times in EU-Startups’ reporting, most recently in September 2026, when it announced a €154.2 million Series B financing round.  The financing is intended to expand the company’s production capabilities and bring its reversible energy systems to additional industrial customers. Total funding sits at €228 million ($256 million).

Berlin-based C1 Green Chemicals

  • Founded in 2022, is developing new chemical production processes using advanced catalysis. Its initial commercial focus is renewable methanol, which can replace fossil-derived methanol in industrial manufacturing and serve as an alternative fuel for shipping.
  • In March 2025, EU-Startups covered C1 Green Chemicals’ €20 million financing package, comprising €15 million in investment and €5 million in approved research grants. The financing was intended to support the development of a demonstration plant and accelerate commercialisation. Total funding sits at €25 million.

Completing the startup-associated pilot projects is Germany’s ICODOS and France’s Flying Whales.

Manufacturing Europe’s CleanTech future

The CleanTech manufacturing category includes three startups – all companies previously featured by EU-Startups.

Sweden’s Orbital Systems

  • Founded in Malmö in 2012 by Mehrdad Mahdjoubi following collaboration involving NASA and Lund University, initially gained attention for its water-recycling shower technology.
  • Orbital Systems was featured by EU-Startups in March 2019 as one of ten European CleanTech startups developing solutions for a more sustainable future. Total funding sits at €61 million ($69 million).

  • Established in 2022, is developing a large-scale solar photovoltaic manufacturing facility in Sarreguemines-Hambach, France.

Germany’s Additive Drives

  • Founded in Dresden in 2020 by Philipp Arnold, Axel Helm and Dr Jakob Jung, develops high-efficiency electric motors using a combination of additive manufacturing and conventional production technologies.

The Innovation Fund

The broader Innovation Fund selection reflects the European Commission’s efforts to support technologies at different stages of commercial readiness. The programme includes 12 large-scale, 17 medium-scale, 20 small-scale, 12 CleanTech manufacturing and 16 pilot projects.

According to the Commission, the 77 selected projects could collectively avoid approximately 290 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions during their first ten years of operation. The programme is financed through revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System, which reinvests carbon market proceeds into low-carbon technologies.

The December 2025 call attracted 358 applications requesting €17.5 billion in funding, considerably exceeding the initially available budget of €2.9 billion.

However, selection does not yet constitute a final grant award. The 77 project promoters have been invited to prepare grant agreements with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA), with final funding amounts and contractual arrangements expected to be confirmed in the first quarter of 2027.

Although the precise share of the €3.4 billion that will ultimately support startup-associated projects remains unclear, our findings highlight the involvement of emerging technology companies in Europe’s industrial transition.

]]> Emerald, a London-based preventive healthcare platform, has secured an additional €1.66 million (£1.4 million/$1.85 million) in funding. This brings the company’s total funding to date to €3.44 million (£2.9 million).

The latest funding includes an €832.2k (£700k) grant from Innovate UK, Emerald’s second award from the organisation, together with a further €832.2k (£700k) in venture capital investment secured after the award. All existing investors, along with new backers including Sequel and Highgoal, supported the round, and Emerald’s valuation increased from its previous funding round.

Alexander Badalyan, co-founder and CEO of Emerald, explained, “There’s huge demand for access to simple healthcare tools that move beyond just testing. People want to understand what those results mean and the steps they can take to boost their long-term health – informed by guidance from trusted medical experts.

“A preventative approach to healthcare significantly improves long-term health outcomes by providing a more holistic view of a patient’s health, highlighting potential issues before they become critical, and empowering people to enter the right pathway earlier.

 “Achieving this ambition is a cornerstone of the current Government’s current health agenda – but the NHS cannot deliver this shift alone. Government efforts must be matched with innovative solutions that are able to have widespread reach. Emerald has unlocked access to millions of potential users through its partnerships – with ambitions to become the UK’s go-to platform for long-term health management. This additional funding allows us to build on the demand we’re already seeing, deepen these partnerships, and expand care.”

Founded in 2024, Emerald says its platform combines in-clinic laboratory screening with a digital platform that brings results, wearable data and health history together in one place. This approach helps members identify potential health risks earlier and empowers them to take control of their long-term health.

Explaining its differentiating factor, Emerald notes that traditional health checks capture one moment in time, whereas the UK startup connects comprehensive testing with users’ past results, lifestyle, and wearable data to reveal patterns, priorities, and changes. 

It further notes that every member is paired with a GP who can diagnose, prescribe, and make formal referrals into both private and NHS care where appropriate. 

The company highlighted that it is clinician-founded and Care Quality Commission registered, offering regulated activities including diagnostic and screening procedures and treatment of disease, disorder or injury. The platform is also authorised as a UKCA Class I medical device with the MHRA.

Since the beginning of 2026, the company reported that it has grown its member base tenfold and has now processed more than 100k laboratory tests, with repeat-screening data. According to the startup, this data highlights improvements in cholesterol levels for two out of three users, blood sugar levels dropping by a third, and reduced inflammation amongst members dropping by almost half. In January this year, the company announced the closure of its €1.78 million ($2 million) pre-Seed round. 

Emerald also mentioned that it has significantly expanded its clinical capabilities and, over the last 12 months, it has announced partnerships with Pluxee, Epassi, Yonder and other businesses across the employee benefits, FinTech and fitness sectors to scale its offering. 

With this approach, the company intends to enable employers to include its services as part of their existing benefits offering.

Chris Sawyer, Innovation Lead, Digital Health at Innovate UK, said, “Connecting earlier health insights with appropriate care is an important opportunity for healthcare innovation in the UK. Through this award, we are supporting Emerald’s development of AI-enabled technology designed to help clinicians deliver more personalised, proactive care. We look forward to seeing the project progress and the impact it could have on health outcomes.”

The company plans to use this additional funding to support commercial expansion and further development of its products and clinical services as the platform aims to reach one million members over the next three years. 

The Innovate UK grant will specifically support the expansion of Emerald’s AI applications and underlying technology, with the aim of improving healthcare outcomes across the UK.

]]> XRlabs, the London-based Surgical Intelligence company built by surgeons for surgeons, has raised €7.48 million ($8.4 million) in Seed funding.

The round was led by Playground Global, the DeepTech-focused venture firm based in Palo Alto, with participation from London-based HealthTech investor Eka Ventures. Alongside the fundraise, XRlabs also announced that Omar Ishrak, who led Medtronic as Chairman and CEO from 2011 to 2020 and previously served as chairman of Intel’s board, has joined as Chair of its Board of Directors.

“The best physical AI companies come from people who’ve experienced a problem in their field firsthand and have the deep expertise to know how to fix it,” said Bruce Leak, General Partner at Playground Global.

Founded by practising neurosurgeon Dr. Ali Haddad in 2024, XRlabs is headquartered in London at the London Institute for Healthcare Engineering, with a second office in Palo Alto, California. The company develops modular, device-agnostic software that sits as an external AI layer across the surgical systems hospitals already own.

Its platform uses computer vision and deep learning to transform live video from surgical scopes, navigation telemetry, and pre-operative CT and MRI imaging into a single real-time, anatomy-aware view of each procedure. XRlabs says its platform has been deployed across more than 100 surgical cases on three continents.

The company offers two core products: XRlabs SIM and SurgicalOS. The XRlabs SIM is a patient-specific planning and rehearsal tool that transforms standard CT and MRI scans into interactive 3D reality models or digital twins, while SurgicalOS is an intraoperative intelligence layer that brings the digital twin created in SIM into the live operative view.

The XRlabs SIM and SurgicalOS together form what the company describes as “Pyramid of Surgical Intelligence,” a layered approach to building AI surgical understanding that mirrors how surgeons are trained, starting from anatomy and building toward real-time operative skill.

“Our conviction is that the operating room is the next frontier for physical AI. Surgery generates extraordinary data, yet almost none of it becomes intelligence in the moments that matter most. This financing lets us change that at scale, moving Surgical Intelligence from landmark first cases to foundational infrastructure in every operating room,” said Dr. Haddad, founder and CEO of XRlabs.

The funding comes on the back of major clinical achievements, including first-in-human use of physical AI in cranial neurosurgery, integrated with an ORBEYE 4K 3D exoscope under research conditions and a world-first in AI-designed patient-specific implants, used in the successful separation of craniopagus twins.

XRlabs says it will use the Seed funding to support the buildout of its engineering and clinical teams, advance its products through regulatory pathways in the UK, Europe, and the US, while extending the clinical evidence base at partner institutions globally. The company has also been awarded a compute allocation on the UK AI Research Resource (AIRR), the UK’s national AI compute infrastructure, which supports the development and scaling of its AI capabilities.

The post Copenhagen’s Plinto raises €2.9 million to help finance teams catch and fix errors with AI agents appeared first on EU-Startups.

]]> Plinto, a Copenhagen-based startup building AI for real-time controlling, has secured €2.9 million in pre-Seed funding.

The round was led by People Ventures and Emblem, with participation from a group of business angels. 

“Companies have systems that record every single transaction, but checking whether those transactions actually match agreements and rules is still largely manual. We’re building AI agents that find deviations, investigate them and take action, so errors get fixed,” said Jakob Nielsen, co-founder and CDO of Plinto.

Plinto was founded in early 2025 by Nermina Suljevic, Nielsen, and Sebastian Rehnby, who previously worked for Peakon, the employee engagement platform acquired by US-based Workday in 2021. The company’s CTO Andreas Garnæs is also an alumnus of Peakon. Together, they bring experience across product development, engineering, commercial scaling, and working with large international organisations.

In large organisations, the volume of financial transactions exceeds what finance teams can review manually. This work is handled by controllers, who typically resort to spot checks or end-of-month reconciliations, leaving enough room for errors such as incorrect prices, duplicate invoices, or mismatched deliveries.

Plinto wants to solve this problem with AI agents that sit on top of the systems companies already use, such as ERP, documents, bank, and collaboration tools like Slack or Microsoft Teams.

When a transaction is flagged, Plinto’s agents are designed not only to alert someone but also to investigate, gather evidence, and follow up with relevant people within the organisation and external contacts. Plinto says the agents are capable of contacting a supplier about a wrongful invoice, requesting a credit note or preparing a correction for approval.

It says one of its customers uncovered around 430 deviations per month in a single part of the business. At another customer, the agents identified a duplicate invoice submitted with a different supplier name in the same minute it arrived.

“Many of our customers work with low margins, so even small errors can quickly add up. The problem is that they’re often only discovered after the money has been paid. We want companies to catch and fix errors before they hit the bottom line,” said Suljevic, co-founder and CEO of Plinto.

Plinto platform integrates with major ERP platforms, including Microsoft Business Central, Xero, and Visma, and connects to major Scandinavian banks as well as over 2,700 other banks. It counts paying customers and pilots in logistics, real estate, facility services, and food production. The platform covers both order-to-cash and procure-to-pay workflows, and all data is processed and stored within the EU. Plinto also says it never uses customer data to train AI models.

The company plans to use the pre-Seed funding for product development, bringing on more enterprise customers and making Plinto’s first move outside Denmark. It wants to bring its agents to enterprises beyond its home market and aims to help them find financial errors in real time.

]]> Turbine Capital, a Swedish VC fund focused on early-stage DeepTech companies in the Nordics, announced the final close of its first fund at €54 million (SEK 608 million) and a new industrial investor.

Mycronic joins the fund alongside Saab, Scania, Volvo Cars and Stena, as well as a number of industrial family offices and private investors. Institutional investors in the fund include Saminvest and the European Investment Fund (EIF).

“Closing our first fund at more than SEK 600 million, with an investor base ranging from leading Nordic industry to European institutions, confirms that our model meets a real need. During our first year, we have shown that multi-corporate venture capital works in practice, not just in theory,” says Anders Ösund, Founding & General Partner, Turbine Capital.

Turbine Capital’s final close comes amid several specialised European VC fund announcements in 2026.

In Sweden, Norrsken Evolve reached a €62 million final close, also backed by Saminvest and the European Investment Fund (EIF). Elsewhere in the Nordics, Copenhagen-based The Footprint Firm closed its €76 million climate and DeepTech fund, PSV Tech finalised a €56 million early-stage fund, and Climentum Capital secured a €60 million first close for climate HardTech investments.

France’s 360 Capital also announced an €85 million closing for its research-driven DeepTech fund Poli360 2.

Together with Turbine Capital, these  announcements represent approximately €393 million in reported fund capital.

Source EU-Startups”Mycronic brings cutting-edge expertise in semiconductors and advanced manufacturing that strengthens our entire industrial network. Together with Saab, Scania, Volvo Cars and Stena, we have a base of industrial partners spanning defence, transport, electrification and now also semiconductor technology – exactly the kind of cross-sector platform Europe’s DeepTech companies need to scale,” adds Pär Hedberg, founder of Sting, who also is initiator and co-founder of Turbine Capital.

Since its first close in April 2025, Turbine Capital says they have built a unique Nordic model for cross-sector collaboration in venture capital: close cooperation with seven university-affiliated incubators – ABI, Uminova, UIC, Sting, LEAD, GU Ventures and IDEON – combined with a broad base of industrial investors.

The model gives investors access to early-stage innovation, while portfolio companies gain access to capital, industrial expertise and customers.

As a new investor in Turbine Capital, Mycronic complements the fund’s existing industrial base. Mycronic is a high-tech company engaged in the development, manufacture and marketing of production equipment with high precision and flexibility requirements for the electronics industry.

The company is in a strong growth phase driven by AI-related infrastructure investments, and has at the same time strengthened its presence in defence-related electronics manufacturing. Mycronic brings deep expertise in semiconductor technology, photonics and advanced manufacturing – key areas within Turbine Capital’s investment thesis.

<!DOCTYPE html><html lang="en-US"><head><meta charset="UTF-8"><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"><link rel="pingback" href="https://www.studyineurope.eu/xmlrpc.php"> <style id="sie-lean-layout"> #sie-lean-main { margin: 0; }

 .et_pb_row { position: relative; width: 80%; max-width: 1080px; margin: 0 auto; }
 .et_pb_row_inner { width: 100%; }
 .et_pb_column { position: relative; } </style> <style id="sie-custom-header-inline">/* ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
 SIE Custom Header — v1.1.2
 Zero-CLS, no JavaScript layout shifts.
 No panoramic image — lean 64px nav bar only.
 backdrop-filter is intentionally NOT used on .sie-hdr__bar.
 Any element with backdrop-filter becomes a CSS containing block for
 position:fixed descendants, which would trap the user-ui mobile bottom bar
 (position:fixed; bottom:0) inside the header instead of the viewport.
 ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════ */
/* ── Root variables ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
:root {
 --sie-hdr-brand:       #0056b3;        /* SIE brand blue                      */
 --sie-hdr-brand-light: #1a6fc4;
 --sie-hdr-bar-h:       64px;           /* nav bar height — fixed, prevents CLS */
 --sie-hdr-bar-bg:      #0056b3;        /* solid — no backdrop-filter needed   */
 --sie-hdr-bar-border:  rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.15);
}
/* ── Wrapper ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr {
 width: 100%;
 display: block;
 min-height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 /* Own stacking context so dropdowns render above Divi page content */
 position: relative;
 z-index: 1000;
}
/* ── Navigation bar ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__bar {
 height: var(--sie-hdr-bar-h);
 background: var(--sie-hdr-bar-bg);
 /* NO backdrop-filter here — it would trap position:fixed children
 (user-ui mobile bottom bar) inside this element instead of viewport */
 border-bottom: 1px solid var(--sie-hdr-bar-border);
}
.sie-hdr__inner {
 max-width: 1280px;
 height: 100%;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 24px;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 32px;
}
/* ── Logo ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__logo {
 flex-shrink: 0;
 text-decoration: none;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-img {
 height: 54px;
 width: auto;
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__logo-text {
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 17px;
 font-weight: 700;
 color: #fff;
 letter-spacing: -0.01em;
 white-space: nowrap;
}
/* ── Desktop navigation ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__nav {
 flex: 1;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list {
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
 display: flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list li {
 position: relative;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 display: inline-flex;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 4px;
 padding: 8px 14px;
 font-family: -apple-system, BlinkMacSystemFont, 'Segoe UI', Roboto, sans-serif;
 font-size: 14px;
 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.88);
 text-decoration: none;
 border-radius: 8px;
 transition: background 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;
 white-space: nowrap;
 min-height: 48px; /* WCAG touch target */
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
}
.sie-hdr__nav-list a:hover,
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle:hover,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle {
 background: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.12);
 color: #fff;
}
/* ── Resources dropdown ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: none;
 position: absolute;
 top: calc(100% + 6px);
 left: 0;
 min-width: 240px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 12px;
 box-shadow: 0 12px 40px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.18);
 padding: 8px 0;
 list-style: none;
 margin: 0;
 z-index: 9999;
}
/* CSS-only hover on desktop */
@media (hover: hover) {
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover > .sie-hdr__dropdown,
 .sie-hdr__has-dropdown:focus-within > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
 }
}
/* JS-toggled state (mobile / keyboard) */
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open > .sie-hdr__dropdown {
 display: block;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown li {
 margin: 0;
 padding: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a {
 display: block;
 padding: 10px 18px;
 font-size: 13.5px;
 color: #003B73;
 font-weight: 500;
 border-radius: 0;
 min-height: unset;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown a:hover {
 background: #f0f7ff;
 color: #0b5394;
}
.sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transition: transform 0.2s ease;
}
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown.is-open .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg,
.sie-hdr__has-dropdown:hover .sie-hdr__dropdown-toggle svg {
 transform: rotate(180deg);
}
/* ── Mobile hamburger ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr__hamburger {
 display: none;
 flex-direction: column;
 justify-content: center;
 align-items: center;
 gap: 5px;
 width: 44px;
 height: 44px;
 background: none;
 border: none;
 cursor: pointer;
 padding: 0;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger span {
 display: block;
 width: 22px;
 height: 2px;
 background: #fff;
 border-radius: 2px;
 transition: transform 0.25s ease, opacity 0.25s ease;
}
/* Animate to ✕ when open */
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(1) {
 transform: translateY(7px) rotate(45deg);
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(2) {
 opacity: 0;
}
.sie-hdr__hamburger[aria-expanded="true"] span:nth-child(3) {
 transform: translateY(-7px) rotate(-45deg);
}
/* ── User-UI icon bar integration ────────────────────────────────────────────
 user-ui.php's desktop bar uses position:absolute; top:20px; right:30px — that
 was designed for Divi's header context. Inside our flex .sie-hdr__inner we
 need it as a normal flex child instead.
 Fixed-position children (auth drawer, mobile bar, destinations panel) are
 unaffected — position:fixed is always viewport-relative provided no ancestor
 has backdrop-filter, transform, or perspective (we intentionally avoid all
 three on .sie-hdr__bar).
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── */
.sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 position: static !important;
 top: auto !important;
 right: auto !important;
 flex-shrink: 0;
 margin-left: auto;
}
/* Align our mobile breakpoint (860px) with user-ui's desktop/mobile split */
@media (min-width: 861px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: flex !important;
 }
}
@media (max-width: 860px) {
 .sie-hdr .se-user-menu-wrapper {
 display: none !important;
 }
}
/* Leonardo icon in the nav bar.
 user-ui's default .se-ai-icon is 86×86 px (fine for the mobile bottom bar),
 but that overflows our 64px-tall nav bar. Override to a crisp 36px square —
 the webp source is already high-res so it stays sharp at 2× on retina. */
.sie-hdr .se-ai-icon {
 width:  36px !important;
 height: 36px !important;
 border-radius: 50%;
 object-fit: cover;
}
/* Icon colours inside the header.
 user-ui defaults: map icon is #2f6fed (dark blue) and heart is #F44336 (red).
 The map icon is nearly invisible on our #0056b3 bar — lift all icons to white.
 The heart keeps its red via the !important below so favourited items still pop. */
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon {
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85) !important;
}
.sie-hdr .se-shortlist-link:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-dest-desktop-btn:hover,
.sie-hdr .se-user-icon:hover {
 color: #fff !important;
}
/* Fav heart — keep the red so it reads as "save" */
.sie-hdr .se-fav-desktop-link {

@media (max-width: 860px) {

 }
 .sie-hdr__hamburger {

.sie-field-hero{position: relative; 
 left: 50%;
 right: 50%;
 margin-left: -50vw;
 margin-right: -50vw;
 width: 100vw; 
 min-height: 480px;
 max-height: 560px;
 background-size: cover;
 background-position: center 40%;
 background-repeat: no-repeat; 
 background-color: #003B73;
 overflow: hidden;
 margin-bottom: 0;}
.sie-field-hero--no-image{background: linear-gradient(
 135deg,
 var(--field-color, #003B73) 0%,
 color-mix(in srgb, var(--field-color, #003B73) 65%, #000) 100%
 );}
.sie-field-hero__bg-img{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 width: 100%;
 height: 100%;
 object-fit: cover;
 object-position: center 40%;
 z-index: 0;
 display: block;}
.sie-field-hero__overlay{position: absolute;
 inset: 0;
 z-index: 1;
 background: linear-gradient(
 to top,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.90) 0%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.60) 38%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.25) 65%,
 rgba(0, 20, 50, 0.12) 100%
 );
 display: flex;
 align-items: flex-end;
 padding-bottom: 52px;}
.sie-field-hero__inner{width: 100%;
 max-width: 1100px;
 margin: 0 auto;
 padding: 0 32px;}
.sie-field-hero__label{display: block;

 font-weight: 500;
 color: rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.75);
 margin-bottom: 12px;
 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-hero__label a{color: inherit;
 text-decoration: none;}
.sie-field-hero__label a:hover{color: #fff;
 text-decoration: underline;}

 margin-bottom: 14px;

 letter-spacing: 0.03em;}
.sie-field-category-badge i{font-size: 11px;

.sie-field-hero__title{font-size: clamp(30px, 5vw, 54px);

<h1 class="title-h1 eac-page-title">Conference on the Future of Europe : the future is in your hands</h1>
<span><span>sandoel</span></span>
<span><time datetime="2021-12-07T08:55:30+01:00" title="Tuesday, December 7, 2021 - 08:55">Tue, 12/07/2021 - 08:55</time>

<div class="ecl"><h2><strong>What is the Conference?</strong></h2>

<p>The <strong>Conference on the Future of Europe </strong>is the first transnational discussion with Europeans on how to address Europe’s challenges together. This is an opportunity to think about what citizens and&nbsp; civil society want for the European Union.</p>

<p>&nbsp;</p>
</div>

  <div class="eac-body lc-stripe-wrapper-text"><h2><strong>How does the Conference work?</strong></h2>

<p>Europeans can share ideas via the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Multilingual Digital Platform</a>, and both national and&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/assemblies/citizens-panels" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">European Citizens' Panels</a>. These contributions feed into the&nbsp;<a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/plenary" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference Plenaries</a>.</p>

<p>The Conference&nbsp;offers a new public forum for an open, inclusive, and transparent debate with citizens around a number of key priorities and challenges.</p>

<h2><strong>How can you participate?</strong></h2>

<ul>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]--><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/processes?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">share your own ideas or support others’ ideas</a> on the multilingual digital Conference platform</li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->organise your own events and promote it by adding them to the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/?locale=en&amp;pk_source=pdf_document&amp;pk_medium=link&amp;pk_campaign=europarl" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Conference platform</a></li>
	<li><!--[if !supportLists]--><!--[endif]-->take a look at the <a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/meetings" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">events organised by people across the EU</a></li>
</ul>

<h2><strong>What will the outcome be?</strong></h2>

<p>All of the ideas gathered and reports on events are published on the platform openly and transparently. These reports will then directly influence the discussions in the European Citizens’ Panels as well as in the Plenaries, where citizens will enter into a dialogue with national and European decision makers.</p>

<p>By spring 2022, the Conference will provide guidance on the future of Europe to the European institutions</p>

<p><a href="https://futureu.europa.eu/pages/getinvolved" target="_blank" class=" eac-external-link">Get involved and make your voice heard when it comes to education, culture, youth, sport, and more</a>.</p>

<p>Follow on Twitter at&nbsp;</p>

<ul>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has a strategy and an overarching structure supporting internationalisation</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>

                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The internationalisation strategy is available and prominently displayed on your website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Internationalisation is an important driver for institutional change, and has a great influence on the major activities of a higher education institution (HEI) i.e. education and research. The importance of internationalisation is recognised, and most institutions have a strategy for internationalisation. However, for a strategy to be efficient, and for it to drive the HEI's activities regarding internationalisation, there is a need for its acceptance from across the whole institution. In addition the strategy could also be accessible to external collaborative partners. It is highly important to have the institution's internationalisation and modernisation strategy published and easily accessible to all.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes incoming and outgoing student and staff mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Mobility is important to the development of the institution as a whole as well as for the individual participants. Therefore the HEI should make mobility and international cooperation a central element in its institutional policies, and explicitly and consistently promote and support student and staff mobility. Non-discrimination policies and further emphasis on the promotion of mobility for under-represented groups should also form an integral part of the institutional support structures.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It promotes engagement in European and international cooperation projects</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution's internationalisation strategy and policy should explicitly and consistently promote the development of cooperation with partners in other EU and non-EU countries. The activities and co-operation projects agreed by the HEI should be based on identified needs. In addition they should identify geographical and subject priorities of the internationalisation strategy.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Specific support measures are provided to staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants. For example:  allocation of additional resources, training on intercultural competences and other relevant aspects of the mob</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The institution should allocate additional resources to support staff working at all levels of the institution with outgoing and incoming participants, such as allowing staff adequate time to carry out work with outgoing and incoming participants and providing administrative back-up (e.g. with financial management). Trainings/webinars/projects could be organised on intercultural competences and communication, management of mobility projects’, enhancement of internationalisation at home/intercultural, or other activities suggested by the staff and supported by the hierarchy. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Incentives are provided to staff involved in international activities</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Participation in such international projects should be seen as an important aspect of the professional development of the staff and of the modernisation of the HEI. It should, therefore, be considered a key component in staff evaluation. As part of the institutional modernisation and internationalisation strategy, concrete support measures should be defined at both institutional and departmental levels to encourage and recognise staff participating in such projects, as well as allow adequate time to carry out this work.</p>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution has established a framework of Inter-Institutional Agreements for Erasmus+ mobility</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on areas of mutual interest</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital that Inter-Institutional Agreements are based on areas of mutual interest. These agreements should identify shared quality requirements specific to the planned exchanges, including concrete proposals as to how these activities will contribute to the development of learning and teaching in participating institutions. The involvement of academic staff is key to ensuring that the selection of partners is based on sufficient knowledge of the area. Each HEI should decide who is responsible for initiating, signing and implementing these agreements and the list of responsible persons should be available on the website for contact and consultation purposes.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on the compatibility of study programmes</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>Inter-Institutional Agreements should be based on a comprehensive understanding of the partner HEIs, the compatibility of study programmes, quality levels and standards considered adequate for student and staff mobility activities. For example, selected partners should have learning, teaching and assessment procedures that can be accepted by the sending institution without requiring mobile students to do any additional work or take examinations upon returning from the receiving institution. The compatibility of the programmes should be reflected in the learning outcomes to be achieved.</p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">They are based on shared quality requirements, student and staff selection for mobility and clear timelines at all stages of the mobility</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>A key role of Inter-Institutional Agreements is to set out agreed, shared quality criteria and clear timelines for all stages of the mobility.<br>Shared quality criteria may include, but are not limited to: selection criteria for the nomination of students and staff, recommended language skills, grading systems, measures for preparing, receiving and integrating Erasmus+ participants. These might be expanded with geographic and subject-specific criteria.<br>In terms of the timelines set out for the mobility activities, particular attention should be paid to:</p><ul><li>The nomination of mobile students by the sending HEI,</li><li>The acceptance of nominees, and</li><li>The issuing of the Transcript of Records after the study period abroad by the receiving HEI. This is normally issued within five weeks after the end date of the mobility period.</li></ul>                      </div>

                        <div class="eche-officer-question">Your institution expresses its commitment to equal access and opportunities to mobile participants</div>
                        <div class="eche-report-button-js eche-report-detail-close"><i class="fa fa-plus-circle fa-3x"></i></div>
                    </div>
                </div>
                <div class="eche-officer-question-wrapper eche-report-question-wrapper-show">
                    <div class="eche-report-border"></div>
                    <div classs="eche-officer-must">
                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">There are specific provisions e.g. in the general policies, rules and regulations of the institution</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In signing the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education, the institution agrees to respect <strong>in full</strong> the principles of non-discrimination as set out in the Programme. The institution must clearly demonstrate through its policies, rules and regulations that equal access and opportunities to mobile participants from all backgrounds. Which means that all individuals or groups will be treated equally, irrespective of their characteristics. In accordance with Article 21 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union, there should be no discrimination "based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic features, language, religion or belief, political or any other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation". For more information, see: <a href="http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf">http://www.europarl.europa.eu/charter/pdf/text_en.pdf</a></p>                      </div>
                    <div class="eche-officer-best">
                                                <h3>Best practices</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">The principle - that extra fees are not being charged to incoming mobile students - is implemented</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The receiving institution must <strong>not </strong>charge any type of fees to incoming mobility students for the tuition, registration or examination of these students or for their access to laboratory, library and other facilities offered to local students.<br>In certain cases, however, mobile students may be required to pay small fees for insurance, student unions, use of miscellaneous materials (e.g. photocopies, laboratory products) on the same basis as these are charged to local students. Students should be made aware of these extra costs before the start of mobility. Fees may only be charged in the case of full degree mobility or for students registered in joint degree programmes.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">All students and staff (incoming and outgoing) are treated equally in all academic and service matters</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>In accordance with equal access and opportunities, all students and staff should be treated equally in all academic and service matters. Clear appeal procedures should be in place to ensure equal treatment. There should be individuals - such as mentors and counsellors - available to offer support.</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">It provides incoming mobile participants with access to the same services and facilities available to local students and staff</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is vital to ensure that incoming mobility participants have full access to the same services and facilities as local students and staff. For example, mobility participants with special needs can benefit from the support services that the receiving institution offers to its local students and staff.</p>                      </div>

                                                <h3>Must have</h3>
                                                <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That is up-to-date, ECTS based and available on the institution's website</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important for each HEI to produce an online Course Catalogue, which includes detailed, user-friendly and up-to-date information on the institution’s educational offer and learning environment to enable students to make the right choices and use their time most efficiently, before and during their study period. The Course Catalogue should follow the guidelines set out in the ECTS Users' Guide (http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm) to increase comparability and transparency. It should be published on the institution's website sufficiently in advance i.e. to enable prospective mobile students to make their choices.</p><p>It should include general information on the institution, its resources and services, as well as academic information on its programmes and individual educational components. The ECTS Users' Guide recommends using the following common structure:</p><ul><li>General information</li><li>Resources and services</li><li>Information on study programmes</li><li>Information on single course units</li></ul><p>The Course Catalogue should also include the names of people to contact, with information about how, when and where to contact them.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That is updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Course Catalogue should be updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices. Ideally, the edition of the Course Catalogue for the upcoming academic year should be available by the early spring of the preceding academic year.</p>                      </div>

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>It is important for each HEI to produce an online Course Catalogue, which includes detailed, user-friendly and up-to-date information on the institution’s educational offer and learning environment to enable students to make the right choices and use their time most efficiently, before and during their study period. The Course Catalogue should follow the guidelines set out in the ECTS Users' Guide (http://ec.europa.eu/education/ects/users-guide/index.htm) to increase comparability and transparency. It should be published on the institution's website sufficiently in advance i.e. to enable prospective mobile students to make their choices.</p><p>It should include general information on the institution, its resources and services, as well as academic information on its programmes and individual educational components. The ECTS Users' Guide recommends using the following common structure:</p><ul><li>General information</li><li>Resources and services</li><li>Information on study programmes</li><li>Information on single course units</li></ul><p>The Course Catalogue should also include the names of people to contact, with information about how, when and where to contact them.&nbsp;</p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">That is updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices</span>
                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The Course Catalogue should be updated regularly and sufficiently in advance for prospective mobile students to make their choices. Ideally, the edition of the Course Catalogue for the upcoming academic year should be available by the early spring of the preceding academic year.</p>                      </div>

                        <h4>Guidance note:</h4>
                         <p>The purpose of the Learning Agreement is to provide a transparent and efficient preparation of the study period abroad and to ensure that the student will receive recognition in his/her degree for the educational components or traineeship successfully completed abroad. The Learning Agreement:</p><ul><li>Sets out the learning outcomes for the mobility, including both the educational components or traineeship activities to be carried out by the student at the receiving institution/organisation/enterprise, which will be recognised by the sending institution upon successful completion of the study programme abroad and counted towards his/her degree.</li><li>Ensures full recognition for satisfactorily completed activities of study mobility and traineeships in terms of credits awarded, without the need for the student to take any further courses or exams, and documents these credits in the student records, so that they can be identified in a transparent way.</li></ul><p>The Learning Agreement is binding for all parties and constitutes the cornerstone of successful student mobility (for studies, traineeships, and combinations thereof), including quality assurances and the process for transparent transfer of credits. It is not compulsory to circulate papers with original signatures; scanned copies of signatures or digital signatures may be accepted, depending on the national legislation.</p><p>The EU official templates for Learning Agreements for studies and traineeships are available online: <a href="http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm">http://ec.europa.eu/education/opportunities/higher-education/quality-framework_en.htm&nbsp;&nbsp;</a></p>                         <span class="eche-officer-user-answer">Including allocation of responsibility to an academic who has the authority to approve, amend and recognise the Learning Agreements on behalf of the responsible academic body</span>
